title: Who Owns the Stack? Governance And Control of Open source AI
affiliations: and University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne)

detail.title: Who Owns the Stack? Governance And Control of Open source AI

declarations.funderStatement: Peukert acknowledges support from the Swiss National Science Foundation for the project 100013_97807.

detail.abstract: Open source software underpins modern artificial intelligence (AI) development, yet the governance of this critical infrastructure remains poorly understood. We analyze 2.3 million AI-related GitHub repositories to map the relationship between contributions and institutional control in the open source AI ecosystem. We document structural decoupling: while a small set of corporate-owned frameworks occupy central positions in the dependency network, the majority of maintenance work on these projects is carried out by independent, unaffiliated contributors. Using network analysis and commit-level attribution data, we show that governance control is highly concentrated even as contribution patterns remain distributed. Methodologically, we contribute a system-level measurement of the AI technology stack by combining dependency-network centrality with a co-dependency map that recovers functional layers from observed joint usage. The separation between who governs the infrastructure and who maintains it raises questions about the long-term sustainability and control of open source AI. We discuss implications for competition and innovation policy and highlight the role of institutional responses such as neutral foundation stewardship and diversified maintainer representation to better align control structures with the distributed nature of open source collaboration.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of Nepal's digital marketplace has heightened the need for an effective and responsive consumer protection regime. Grounded in the Consumer Protection Act, 2018, Nepal's legal framework guarantees fundamental consumer rights, including safety, access to information, choice, and redress. Enforcement is shared among multiple regulators, notably the Department of Commerce, Nepal Rastra Bank, and the Nepal Insurance Authority. A major institutional milestone is the establishment of the Consumer Court in March 2025, marking a shift from largely quasijudicial mechanisms to a specialized judicial forum for consumer dispute resolution. This article examines the statutory foundations of consumer protection, the evolving role of sector-specific regulators in digital and financial markets, and emerging jurisprudential trends of the Consumer Court, including high-compensation medical negligence cases. While recent reforms have strengthened judicial access and oversight, challenges persist in consumer awareness, regulatory coordination, and adapting enforcement to digital market complexities. The article emphasizes the need for enhanced consumer education, institutional strengthening, and coordinated regulatory action.

detail.abstract: Major crises such as COVID-19 and natural disasters fundamentally change the way people shop and make the purchasing decisions. The paper will discuss the psychological and social forces that motivate consumer behavior in case of emergencies based on the available academic research. Our results revealed that stockpiling behavior is motivated by fear, uncertainty, and perceived risk, but not by the conventional promotions and discounts. Social media also drives panic by use of social proof and lack of trust in institutional communication only adds anxiety to consumers. These crises cause permanent changes in behavior: buyers quickly start using online shopping, giving more attention to basic items, and creating new spending habits, oriented to safety and supply. In the case of businesses, to survive such disruptions, businesses should go beyond the normal marketing strategies. The keys to success lie in establishing trust, maintaining open communication in the supply chains, digital transformation, and suitability of value propositions to meet the basic needs of security and peace of mind of the consumers in an uncertain world.

title: Supply Chain Disruption and Consumer Purchasing Behavior During the 2025 Sri Lankan Disaster: Examining Panic Buying and Price Fluctuations
affiliations: Uwa Wellassa University of Sri Lanka, Uwa Wellassa University of Sri Lanka, Uwa Wellassa University of Sri Lanka, Uwa Wellassa University of Sri Lanka and Uwa Wellassa University of Sri Lanka

detail.title: Supply Chain Disruption and Consumer Purchasing Behavior During the 2025 Sri Lankan Disaster: Examining Panic Buying and Price Fluctuations
detail.abstract: Economic systems are abruptly disrupted by natural disasters, especially supply chains that guarantee the continual provision of necessities. Transportation networks, retail distribution, and inventory replenishment systems were all negatively impacted by Sri Lanka's 2025 floods and landslides. With a focus on panic buying, stockpiling, and transient price swings, this study investigates how these supply chain disturbances affected customer purchase behavior. According to earlier research, uncertainty and supply shortages greatly boost panic-driven buying, which exacerbates demand volatility and short-term inflation (Wu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). These effects are further amplified by psychological factors as anxiety, perceived shortage, and herd mentality (Saral, 2024). This paper offers empirical findings pertinent to disaster-prone developing economies like Sri Lanka, drawing on well-established supply chain and consumer behavior literature. It also offers management and policy recommendations to reduce market volatility during future crises.

title: Consumer Behaviour during the COVID-19 Pandemic and Marketing Strategies Adopted by Business Organizations
affiliations: , Uva Wellassa University - Uva Wellassa University, Faculty of Management, Students, Uva Wellassa University - Uva Wellassa University, Faculty of Management, Students, Uva Wellassa University - Uva Wellassa University, Faculty of Management, Students and Uva Wellassa University - Uva Wellassa University, Faculty of Management, Students

detail.title: Consumer Behaviour during the COVID-19 Pandemic and Marketing Strategies Adopted by Business Organizations
detail.abstract:
The COVID-19 pandemic represents one of the most disruptive global disasters in
modern history, profoundly affecting consumer behaviour and business operations.
This paper reviews existing literature on consumer behaviour during the COVID-19
pandemic, with particular emphasis on panic buying, stockpiling, herd mentality,
media influence, and shifts in discretionary spending. The review further examines
the marketing strategies adopted by business organizations in response to these
behavioral changes, including digital and social media marketing, transparent
communication, flexible pricing, supply chain adaptation, and ethical marketing
practices. Drawing on both international and Sri Lankan studies, the paper highlights
how fear, uncertainty, and perceived scarcity shaped consumer purchasing decisions
during COVID-19, while organizational resilience depended on adaptive, technology-
driven, and trust-oriented marketing strategies. The findings indicate that businesses
prioritizing continuity, fairness, and long-term customer relationships were better
positioned to manage market disruptions during the pandemic. This review
contributes to strategic marketing literature by integrating consumer behaviour
insights with crisis marketing responses specific to the COVID-19 context.

title: Consumer Behaviour within the Face of COVID-19 Pandemic and Natural Disasters
affiliations: Uva Wellassa University, Uva Wellassa University, Uva Wellassa University, Uva Wellassa University and Uva Wellassa University

detail.title: Consumer Behaviour within the Face of COVID-19 Pandemic and Natural Disasters
detail.abstract: Consumer behaviour and market dynamics have been greatly affected by disasters like pandemics and natural catastrophes as they bring about uncertainty, fear, and scarcity perception. The COVID-19 pandemic alongside the floods and landslides that ravaged Sri Lanka in 2021, disrupted daily consumption patterns like never before. Panic buying, stockpiling, switching brands, and increased reliance on digital channels were some of the trigger behaviours. The paper investigates consumer behaviour in the occurrence of disasters and evaluates the marketing strategies that were employed by companies in response to the changes in consumer behaviour. Based on a thorough review of both international and local literature, this study merges the evidence from both pandemic and natural disaster scenarios to discover the main psychological, social, and situational factors that drive consumer behaviour. The results show that firms that applied adaptive, ethical, and consumer-oriented marketing practices such as open communication, fair pricing, supply chain flexibility, and online interaction were more likely to win consumer trust and keep their operations running. This research combines pandemic and natural disaster viewpoints within one analytical framework to contribute disaster marketing literature and also provide practical insights for the managers working in unstable environments.

title: Three Tiers and Thresholds: Incentives in Private Market Investing
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School and

detail.title: Three Tiers and Thresholds: Incentives in Private Market Investing
detail.abstract: This paper studies optimal contract design in private market investing, focusing on internal decision making in venture capital and private equity firms. A principal relies on an agent who privately exerts costly due diligence effort and then recommends whether to invest. Outcomes are observable ex post even when an opportunity is declined, allowing compensation to reward both successful investments and prudent decisions to pass. We characterize profit maximizing contracts that induce information acquisition and truthful reporting. We show that three tier contracts are sufficient, with payments contingent on the agent's recommendation and the realized return. In symmetric environments satisfying the monotone likelihood ratio property, the optimal contract further simplifies to a threshold contract that pays only when the recommendation is aligned with an extreme realized return. These results provide guidance for performance based compensation that promotes diligent screening while limiting excessive risk taking.

title: Evolution and Efficiency of Agricultural Utilization Wastewaters Management Chain in Bulgaria
affiliations: Institute of Agricultural Economics

detail.title: Evolution and Efficiency of Agricultural Utilization Wastewaters Management Chain in Bulgaria

declarations.funderStatement: This study has been funded by the BulgarianScience Fund, the project "Agricultural land, green transformation, energy transition, digital environment" , Contract No КП-06-Н96/2 from 9.12.2025.

detail.abstract: There has been a fundamental modernization of the wastewater management system in Bulgaria during the EU pre-accession and membership periods. Transition toward sustainable management of wastewaters has been associated with modern disposal of generated sludge from wastewater treatment plants and increasing agricultural utilization. Agricultural Utilization Wastewaters Management Chain emerged and gradually extended along with augmentation of the amount of produced sludge and its share effectively used in agriculture. This paper analyses the evolution and challenges of agricultural inclusion in sustainable wastewater management in Bulgaria. It is based on incorporation of the interdisciplinary New Institutional Economics methodology, official data and numerous in-depth interviews with representatives of the wastewater treatment plants, responsible authorities, farmers participating and not involved in sludge utilization, and other related agents. The study has found out that there has been a significant modernization of formal institutional environment (rules, regulations, standards, agencies) and incentive structure for agricultural sludge production, transportation, and utilization in recent years. Nevertheless, the potential for inclusion of agriculture in water treatment plants' sludge utilization has not been entirely used and policy target in the area effectively reached. The main impediments for the later arethe significant transition and compliance costs for related agents, inadequate public information, training, and support, environmental and health risks, opposition of landowners, businesses, eco-groups and residents, and uncertain directions of policy development. In the future following actions are needed to promote agricultural use of sludge: clearer policies for wastewaters management, waste disposals and agricultural sludge utilization, including development of a national strategy for sludge management; better enforcement of formal regulations and quality standards in agricultural utilization wastewaters management chain; introducing measures to reduce institutionally determined (production and transaction) costs for agents; support specialized training, information and independents assessment on agricultural sludge utilization; use CAP and other EU instruments to support agents' efforts to adapt to formal requirements and extend sustainable treatment, disposal, transportation, agricultural utilization and commercialization of sludge.

title: Algorithmic Governance and Human Discretion in DAOs: A Socio-Technical Analysis

detail.title: Algorithmic Governance and Human Discretion in DAOs: A Socio-Technical Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest associated with this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human participants, patients, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: The author gratefully acknowledges the support of the University of Bologna and the University of Luxembourg, which made this research possible.

detail.abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) are often presented as a transformative alternative to traditional organizational and governance models, promising rule-based coordination, transparency, and decentralization through blockchain-enabled automation. By encoding decision-making and execution into smart contracts, DAOs are commonly portrayed as minimizing human discretion and displacing hierarchical authority. Yet nearly a decade of empirical experience reveals a more complex reality. DAO governance is neither fully autonomous nor purely algorithmic, but instead unfolds through a persistent interaction between on-chain code and off-chain human coordination. This article advances the central claim that DAOs should be understood as hybrid socio-technical governance systems structured by an enduring duality between algorithmic authority and human judgment. Drawing on theories of network governance, socio-legal institutionalism, and political constitutionalism, the paper examines how DAOs operationalize governance through code while simultaneously reproducing familiar dynamics of power concentration, discretion, and emergency authority. Rather than eliminating governance, DAOs reconfigure it across layered technical, economic, and social domains. The analysis proceeds in three steps. First, it situates DAOs within the broader evolution of governance from hierarchies and markets toward network-based coordination. Second, it analyzes the dual architecture of DAO governance by distinguishing between on-chain execution mechanisms and off-chain deliberative processes, with particular attention to consensus and voting systems as instruments of algorithmic coordination. Third, it identifies recurring governance pathologies, including plutocratic voting, governance attacks, rigidity, and legitimacy deficits, that challenge normative claims of decentralization and self-rule. The article concludes that DAOs do not represent post-governance organizations, but experimental institutional forms whose stability depends on reconciling algorithmic efficiency with legitimacy, accountability, and adaptability. By foregrounding the limits of "code as law," the paper contributes to contemporary debates on algorithmic governance, digital constitutionalism, and the future of collective decision-making in blockchain-based systems.

title: Warner Bros as Antitrust’s Streaming Stress Test
affiliations: University of Arizona

detail.title: Warner Bros as Antitrust’s Streaming Stress Test
detail.abstract:
Warner Bros. Discovery’s planned breakup and the resulting bidding war pitting Netflix against Paramount Skydance provide a rare, real-time stress test for antitrust merger review in contemporary media ecosystems, where scale, data, and portfolio breadth shape competitive dynamics. Warner Bros’s content library, franchises, production capabilities, and distribution infrastructure are competitively consequential across interdependent markets, including theatrical distribution and exhibition, subscription and ad-supported streaming, content licensing and windowing, advertising, and talent. A shift in control over these assets would therefore reverberate beyond any single line of business, reshaping rivalry and bargaining leverage across multiple markets at once.

This article observes that, historically, bidders’ appetites for prized media enterprises have repeatedly fueled undue optimism about the feasibility of successful integration. It identifies four domains in which twentieth-century antitrust doctrines and evidentiary conventions may impede courts’ ability to assess twenty-first-century economic realities: (1) market-by-market analysis in multi-market ecosystems; (2) thin pools of viable buyers; (3) uncertainty about the operational success of proposed mergers and the appropriate “but-for” baseline; and (4) the domestic competitive effects of globally scaled operations and multi-jurisdictional oversight.

detail.title: Health at the Margins: How Historical Ethnic Borders Shape Contemporary Outcomes

No new data were collected from human participants, and no individually identifiable information was accessed. Accordingly, the study did not require institutional ethics approval. detail.abstract: This study investigates how historical ethnic borders-precolonial demarcations that continue to structure institutional and geographic realities-shape contemporary health outcomes in Africa. Drawing on high-resolution geospatial data, Demographic and Health Surveys, and a digitized version of Murdock's map of ethnic homelands, we demonstrate that regions near historical ethnic borders face significantly worse health outcomes, including greater reliance on unimproved water and sanitation infrastructure, higher child morbidity and mortality, lower vaccination uptake, and diminished access to maternal health services. To address potential endogeneity, we implement a novel instrumental variable strategy using Voronoi-generated theoretical borders, enabling us to isolate the causal impact of ethnic border exposure. We identify several pathways driving these disparities: institutional fragmentation, geographic isolation, lower public goods provision, and increased exposure to conflict and resource competition. Our findings underscore that historical spatial inequalities continue to shape modern health disparities, offering a new lens for understanding and addressing persistent health inequities in low-and middle-income countries.

title: Taking Stock of Democracy: Abnormal Returns of High-Profile Members of Congress
affiliations: and Dartmouth College - Department of Economics

detail.title: Taking Stock of Democracy: Abnormal Returns of High-Profile Members of Congress

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available data and involved no human subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: As public trust in Congress declines, Congressional stock trading has once again become the subject of public policy recommendations and news headlines. This paper tracks Congressional returns on the stock market over time, focusing on the returns of the top 15 stock traders by volume. In particular, we isolate 2020 as a benchmark for the evaluation of buy-and-hold abnormal returns. In January of 2020, four Senators were publicly involved in insider trading scandals preceding the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, but all investigations were dropped by the Department of Justice. We hypothesize that the existing legal framework's deterrent effect may have weakened following these events. This would predict decreased risk aversion and higher Congressional returns on the stock market, especially for high-volume traders. We find that while Congress does not significantly outperform the market at any point in time, mean buy-and-hold abnormal returns for both Congress writ large and high-volume traders have increased at the 20-, 60-, and 127-day benchmarks. Additionally, the standard deviations of both of the aforementioned categories have grown over time, demonstrating wider variance in stock market performance for members of Congress from 2020-2023 relative to 2012-2020.

title: Are Dividends Relevant for Capital Structure? Worldwide Evidence of the Institutional Framework
affiliations: Universidad de Valladolid - Department of Finance and Accounting, Universidad de Valladolid and University of Valladolid - Department of Financial Economics and Accounting

detail.title: Are Dividends Relevant for Capital Structure? Worldwide Evidence of the Institutional Framework

declarations.funderStatement: The Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities (projects PID2023-150140NA-I00 and PID2024-155796NB-I00).

detail.abstract: In the context of tighter external financing conditions and persistent shareholder pressure for dividends-both in the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis and amid ongoing geopolitical tensions-we examine how dividend payments affect corporate financial leverage. We further test whether four institutional factors shape this relationship, as dividends reduce internal funds, while the institutional context determines access to external financing. Using a sample of 36,995 listed non-financial companies from 41 countries, we find that dividends positively influence leverage, but the magnitude of this effect depends on country-specific factors. Specifically, institutional quality, financial development, and global economic policy uncertainty amplify the dividendleverage link, whereas dividend taxation dampens it. Taken together, our results highlight the need to account for institutional settings when analyzing how dividends affect firms' capital structure decision.

detail.title: Ethics of AI

publicationDetails.detailsText: Tartaro, A., and Héder, M. (2025). Ethics of AI. In Elgar Encyclopedia of Political Communication (pp. 529–532). Edward Elgar Publishing. https://doi.org/10.4337/9781035301447.vol1.00132

detail.abstract: This entry presents a comprehensive overview of AI ethics, delving into various ethical and social issues arising from AI's expanding role in different facets of private and societal life. It sheds light on critical challenges such as accountability gaps, biases, discrimination, and risks associated with generative AI technologies which are relevant for information flows and the public communication system. The entry then explores the emergence of concepts like Trustworthy AI and Responsible AI as responses to these challenges, underscoring their importance in developing AI systems that minimize risks and maximize societal benefits. Despite the growing optimism around Trustworthy AI, the entry also emphasizes the difficulties in implementing ethical principles within AI systems. This opens the discussion to critical perspectives that, while not mainstream in AI ethics, offer valuable insights into power dynamics inherent in AI technologies. Furthermore, the article addresses the ongoing debate on AI regulation and standardization, framing it as an extension of the initial AI ethics discourse. Lastly, it outlines the relevance of analyzing public and political discourse on AI to scholars and practitioners in the field of political communication.

title: Do Marriage and Childbirth Change Time Preferences? Evidence from Japanese Panel Data

detail.title: Do Marriage and Childbirth Change Time Preferences? Evidence from Japanese Panel Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Time preference is a core economic concept. Although classical models assume that time preferences are exogenous and stable, recent research suggests that they are shaped endogenously and can shift in response to life events. However, the potential impacts of two universal life events, marriage and childbirth, remain largely unexplored. This study empirically examines how individuals' time preferences change following marriage and childbirth, using 13 years of nationally representative Japanese panel data. Employing individual fixed-effects models, we estimate within-person changes in time discount rates in the year after each event. The results show that marriage is not significantly associated with time discount rates, whereas childbirth increases these rates in the short run, particularly among men. These findings provide new empirical evidence on the dynamic and context-dependent nature of time preferences and highlight the importance of timing-sensitive policy interventions to support effective decision making and family wellbeing during major life transitions.

title: Hospital Leadership and Support System: In Relation to Mental Health of Registered Radiologic Technologists
affiliations: CORE Gateway College Inc. and CORE Gateway College Inc.

detail.title: Hospital Leadership and Support System: In Relation to Mental Health of Registered Radiologic Technologists
detail.abstract: This research determines the leadership styles, support system, and mental health of registered Radiologic Technologists (RRTs) at Dr. Paulino J. Garcia Memorial Research and Medical Center (DPJGMRMC). The study used a descriptive-correlational research design. A total of 30 RRTs served as the final respondents of the study. The data gathered were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. The results indicated that among the three categories of leadership of administrators, the dominance of democratic leadership was more prevalent in the workplace. Moreover, organizational support was higher compared to peer support and received a rating of strongly agreed. There were also reported mild levels of stress, anxiety and depression among the respondents. Correlation analysis indicated that leadership style, support systems and mental health of the respondents had significant relationship. The paper identifies that mental health risks and workplace well-being can be mitigated through the enhancement of leadership practices and support systems among medical imaging professionals.

title: Determinants of Local Government Financial Report Quality: The Moderating Role of Organizational Commitment in Minahasa Regency
affiliations: Sam Ratulangi University, Sam Ratulangi University, Sam Ratulangi University, Sam Ratulangi University, Sam Ratulangi University and University of Debrecen

detail.title: Determinants of Local Government Financial Report Quality: The Moderating Role of Organizational Commitment in Minahasa Regency
detail.abstract: This study investigates the determinants of local government financial report quality in Minahasa Regency by examining the influence of human resource competence, information technology usage, and internal control systems, as well as the moderating role of organizational commitment. Grounded in Agency Theory and Stewardship Theory, the research argues that high‐ quality financial reporting is essential to fulfilling public accountability, ensuring transparency, and strengthening governance in local government entities. Using a quantitative approach, data were collected from civil servants involved in financial management across regional work units and analyzed using Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results demonstrate that human resource competence, information technology usage, and internal control systems each have a significant positive effect on the quality of local government financial reports. Furthermore, organizational commitment is found to strengthen several of these relationships, confirming its role as an important moderating variable in enhancing financial reporting quality. These findings highlight that technical capacity alone is insufficient; organizational dedication and adherence to shared values are also crucial in ensuring reliable, relevant, comparable, and understandable financial information. This study contributes to the literature by integrating organizational commitment as a moderating factor within the context of government financial reporting, offering empirical support for both Agency and Stewardship perspectives. Practically, the results emphasize the need for local governments to invest in human capital development, strengthen information systems, improve internal control mechanisms, and cultivate strong organizational commitment to maintain and enhance the quality of financial reporting.

title: Determinants and Life-Cycle Effects of Survival Ambiguity
affiliations: Lund University and HEC Montreal

detail.title: Determinants and Life-Cycle Effects of Survival Ambiguity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Neither of the authors has any relationship to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: We have obtained ethics approval for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge fi nancial support from the Swiss National Science Foundation.

detail.abstract: Sound retirement planning requires individuals to have precise beliefs about their survival chances. Based on an online survey experiment administered to a representative sample of the US population, we provide first evidence of the patterns of individuals' uncertainty about their survival probabilities, i.e., survival ambiguity, over the life-cycle. To this end, we devise a novel direct measure of survival ambiguity at the individual level, using the variance of the distribution of subjective survival probabilities. Leveraging experimental variation, we find that providing information about objective survival chances decreases individuals' degree of survival ambiguity. Further, we show that individuals' survival ambiguity is strongly negatively associated with individuals' savings rates. Finally, we provide a realistic life-cycle model of savings and portfolio choice that rationalizes the empirical evidence. Our findings provide an explanation for the observation that many individuals "save too little" for their retirement and support information campaigns about individuals' objective survival chances in addition to financial education programs to improve retirement security, as survival ambiguity presents a previously unexplored determinant of financial well-being.

title: Is there a Place for Local Content Requirements in EU Public Procurement?
affiliations: University of Zagreb Faculty of Law

detail.title: Is there a Place for Local Content Requirements in EU Public Procurement?
detail.abstract: Local content requirements (LCRs) represent the practice of prioritising domestic economic inputs within the national market. In the context of public procurement, this approach is typically observed when preference is given to local resources and economic operators during the evaluation and scoring of tenders, or even when only local economic operators are allowed to participate in the public procurement procedure. This Chapter examines the potential for incorporating LCR provisions within EU public procurement procedures. The analysis is divided into two main perspectives. Firstly, it considers the concept of LCRs and the feasibility of implementing such provisions from the standpoint of individual Member States. Secondly, it explores the issue at the broader EU level, evaluating the compatibility and implications of LCRs within the framework of European Union regulations and policies.

title: Rural and Community Development Toward Food Security and Poverty Alleviation: Institutional Lessons from SEARCA
affiliations: and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Rural and Community Development Toward Food Security and Poverty Alleviation: Institutional Lessons from SEARCA
detail.abstract: Food insecurity and rural poverty remain persistent challenges in Southeast Asia despite decades of agricultural and rural development. Community-based initiatives achieve short-term gains but face difficulties in sustaining outcomes. From a human ecology perspective, these challenges reflect complex interactions among communities, institutions, and environmental systems, highlighting the need to examine institutional processes that shape development practice. This study examines the experience of the Southeast Asian Regional Center for Graduate Study and Research in Agriculture in communitybased rural development related to food security and poverty alleviation over several decades. Using a qualitative institutional synthesis of selected projects, the analysis draws on project documents and program records to identify recurring strategies, enabling conditions, and constraints across diverse social-ecological contexts. The findings show that initiatives emphasizing participatory processes, strong linkages with local governments and academic institutions, capacity development, value chain engagement, and ecosystem-based planning are more likely to support durable outcomes. By situating institutional practice within community-environment interactions, this study contributes to the CHE@50 Special Issue by illustrating how co-created pathways in human ecology shape sustainable development outcomes. The study concludes that meso-level institutions are critical in mediating communityinstitution-environment interactions and offers lessons for community-based initiatives in similar settings.

title: Temporal Concentration Effects of Mergers: Beyond HHI and Static Thresholds
affiliations: Turkish Competition Authority

detail.title: Temporal Concentration Effects of Mergers: Beyond HHI and Static Thresholds
detail.abstract: Measures of market concentration, particularly the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), remain central to merger screening and enforcement. Conventional merger guidelines typically rely on static thresholds and HHI triggers to flag transactions that may pose competitive concerns. Although these measures offer transparency and ease of implementation, a growing body of work highlights that static concentration measures may be conceptually insufficient. HHI-based screens assume that concentration is both an adequate proxy for unilateral market power and that its competitive relevance is captured at the moment of merger. In practice, however, concentration may adjust immediately, gradually, or with substantial delay as firms reorganize capacity, realign cost structures, or modify operational strategies. This paper presents an empirical framework that captures temporal post-merger concentration trajectories, rather than relying on the HHI levels or a single ∆HHI snapshot. Using a time-series design combined with principal component analysis (PCA), the study extracts a latent factor that summarizes non-merger macroeconomic and cost pressures common to all firms and estimating a Newey-West corrected event-window model in which post-merger months are grouped into early, mid-term, and long-term phases, allowing to isolate the timing and magnitude of merger-induced concentration changes. Results reveal that, after accounting for common shocks, HHI does not exhibit a significant increase in the early-term and statistically robust rises in concentration appears only in the mid and long-term, suggesting that structural adjustments, such as capacity consolidation or strategic retrenchment might materialize gradually rather than instantaneously. These findings also underscore the alternative extension of static HHI-based analysis, which may overlook competitive effects that unfold over extended horizons. By documenting the time-varying evolution of concentration, the analysis highlights the need for merger assessment frameworks that incorporate temporal patterns of market structure to more accurately capture the competitive impact of mergers.

title: Eurasian Integration and Civilizational Self-Determination of the Countries of Central Eurasia
affiliations: The Odintsovo Branch of MGIMO University

detail.title: Eurasian Integration and Civilizational Self-Determination of the Countries of Central Eurasia
detail.abstract: When we speak of Central Eurasia, we inevitably mean not only a geographical but, above all, a civilizational category. This space-from the Urals to the Altai, from the Sayan Mountains to the Himalayas-has always been a meeting point of great cultures, religions, and traditions. A unique type of social order and political culture developed here, one that cannot be understood without the idea of mutual respect, synthesis, and dialogue.

title: Structuring and Executing Real Estate Transactions - A Comparative Study of M&A, Private Equity Investments, Joint Ventures, and Due Diligence in India, The United States, The United Kingdom, Canada, and Singapore
affiliations: Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University

detail.title: Structuring and Executing Real Estate Transactions - A Comparative Study of M&A, Private Equity Investments, Joint Ventures, and Due Diligence in India, The United States, The United Kingdom, Canada, and Singapore
detail.abstract: In a contemporary context, real estate transactions have transformed into intricately structured, multi-layered and capital-expensive contracts due to globalization, cross-border investments, and the diversification of governing regulations. This work attempts a comparative analysis of the structure and execution of real estate transactions using four main vehicles, mergers and acquisitions (M & A), private equity, joint ventures, and due diligence across five jurisdictions, India, United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Singapore. This body of research positions real estate at the nexus of property law, corporate law, financial regulation, and investing. It examines how different financial legal structures governing the property affect transactions in the real estate market by considering the legal architecture of a jurisdiction in determining efficiency, default risk, and confidence of the market. The study explains the differences and contrasts between the emerging and sophisticated market by examining the law, theory, and practice. Most jurisdictions, such as the United States, United Kingdom, and Singapore, have a high degree of legal certainty, digitalized land registries, and due diligence frameworks. India, on the other hand, has structural challenges to do with the fragmentation of land records, overlapping regulatory structures, and slow moving procedures, as India has recently developed the real estate market regulatory framework with the establishment of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016. Canada has developed an intermediate model of real estate with a high degree of provincial regulatory and legislative autonomy, strong market protection for investors, and growing dominance of environmental and indigenous rights. The results of the study show that the correlation between the regulation of properties and the structuring of corporate entities leads to the success of a transaction. There is a greater level of market transparency and cross-border movement of capital in the Jurisdictions that have technologically advanced integrated regulatory systems. The research developed a concluding best practices and suggests a syncronised legal framework that can bolster real estate investment in India while maintaining a Regulatory balance, market fluidity, and protection of the Investors.

title: From Transparency to Prediction: Quantifying the Drivers of Physician Reimbursement Variation
affiliations: Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center

detail.title: From Transparency to Prediction: Quantifying the Drivers of Physician Reimbursement Variation

declarations.ethicsApproval: Publicly available data used, no IRB needed.

detail.abstract: The implementation of the Transparency in Coverage (TiC) rule in 2022 required commercial payers to publicly disclose negotiated reimbursement rates, fundamentally expanding access to pricing data in U.S. healthcare. However, while this policy increased transparency, published rate data alone does not explain why reimbursement varies across physicians and specialties, nor does it enable prediction of future payer behavior. Using national Transparency in Coverage data combined with specialty-level physician workforce and economic characteristics, this study models variation in commercial reimbursement for identical evaluation and management services. Focusing on commonly billed outpatient visit codes, we quantify how structural, economic, and training-related features of physician specialties influence negotiated reimbursement. This approach transforms transparency data from descriptive reporting into predictive insight, enabling providers and health systems to better anticipate payer dynamics and inform data-driven contracting and workforce decisions.

title: Mandatory Supply Chain Due Diligence and Firm Performance: Evidence from the French Loi De Vigilance
affiliations: ESCP Business School and Arizona State University (ASU)

detail.title: Mandatory Supply Chain Due Diligence and Firm Performance: Evidence from the French Loi De Vigilance

keywords: Loi de Vigilance (French Duty of Vigilance Law)

detail.abstract: We study how mandatory supply-chain due diligence affects firms' input costs, output scale and operational efficiency, using France's Loi de Vigilance-a regulation requiring large firms to set up a process to identify and mitigate human-rights and environmental risks in their supply chains starting in 2018 fiscal year reporting. We leverage a dynamic diffusion model in which compliance propagates gradually through the supply base to examine how the regulatory obligations shaped firms' performance dynamics over time. Using a generalized synthetic triple-difference design with interactive fixed effects, we compare 73 publicly listed firms subject to the law with matched firms from eight European economies over 2006-2023. In the short run, the law increased firms' input-cost intensity (COGS/Assets), reflecting upfront compliance expenditures; in the long run, these costs dissipated. Operational efficiency (COGS/Sales) improved steadily, declining by roughly 10% over the post-treatment period, while effects on output scale (Sales/Assets) remained modest. Efficiency gains are stronger for product firms, firms with larger supplier bases, and firms exhibiting higher compliance levels with the regulation. Overall, the results suggest that mandatory supply chain due-diligence regulations did not hurt firms and can even promote long-run operational efficiency. This study provides the first dynamic evaluation of a mandatory due-diligence regime and offers policy guidance for calibrating firm-size and supplier-based thresholds under the forthcoming EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive.

title: Structuring and Executing Real Estate Transactions - A Comparative Study of M&A, Private Equity Investments, Joint Ventures, and Due Diligence in India, The United States, The United Kingdom, Canada, and Singapore
affiliations: Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University

title: When AI Mirrors Too Well: Frame Amplification, Feedback Loops, and the Hidden Failure Mode of Empathetic Systems

detail.title: When AI Mirrors Too Well: Frame Amplification, Feedback Loops, and the Hidden Failure Mode of Empathetic Systems
detail.abstract: As conversational AI systems increasingly optimize for contextual awareness and emotional fluency, they introduce a distinct and rarely theorized risk known as Frame Amplification. While standard alignment research focuses on hallucination or bias, this paper examines excessively adaptive mirroring. This is a phenomenon where an AI system infers the transient cognitive or emotional frame of a user and reflects it back with increased linguistic precision and coherence. Drawing on control theory and human factors analysis, we argue that this interaction acts as a high gain positive feedback loop. Unlike human interlocutors, whose validation is constrained by social friction and independent agency, AI models optimize for minimum latency and maximum relevance. This creates Synthetic Resonance, which is an unconstrained alignment that can unintentionally stabilize harmful user states, such as hopelessness, paranoia, or rigid narratives of self, by validating them as objective reality. We distinguish between Affective Validation, which acknowledges state, and Cognitive Endorsement, which confirms interpretation. We propose that current reward models dangerously conflate the two. Finally, we outline a governance framework for Safe Mirroring Envelopes. These are design constraints that rate limit resonance in vulnerable contexts to preserve human epistemic agency.

title: Developing Economic Cooperation between Russia and Mongolia as a Way to Strengthen Intercivilizational Dialogue
affiliations: The Odintsovo Branch of MGIMO University

detail.title: Developing Economic Cooperation between Russia and Mongolia as a Way to Strengthen Intercivilizational Dialogue
detail.abstract: The partnership demonstrates resilience and adaptability, with future prospects hinging on the diversification of Mongolia's export basket, the realization of joint infrastructure and tourism initiatives, and the deepening of institutional, regional, and humanitarian integration. The shift to national currency settlements provides a critical foundation for this long-term strategic engagement.

title: Perceptions of Group Norms and Conformism in Preferences for Exclusion in India
affiliations: Ashoka University, New York University and Department of Political Science, Yale University

detail.title: Perceptions of Group Norms and Conformism in Preferences for Exclusion in India

declarations.ethicsApproval: The protocols for human subjects research were exempted from full review by the Yale University IRB.

detail.abstract: Is support for anti-minority policies and rhetoric shaped by the perception that coethnics favor minority exclusion? Through a pair of survey experiments, we find that Hindu respondents in India perceive other Hindus to be far more exclusionary towards minorities than they are themselves. We also find strong evidence of conformism to perceived public opinion. When presented with information about majority public opinion, respondents update their beliefs in the direction of the information provided, regardless of whether it portrays others as exclusionary or inclusionary. Indeed, mere reference of the religious ingroup is sufficient to induce conformism: when respondents are asked to think about other Hindus' opinions about an issue, they express individual opinions that are significantly closer to the perceived majority opinion than otherwise. Elucidating these patterns contributes to our understanding of how distortions of public opinion can shape individual preferences about minority exclusion.

title: How Do Sustainable Literacies Shape Individual Sustainable Behaviors? A European Analysis
affiliations: University of Parma - Dipartimento di Scienze Economiche e Aziendali, Catholic University of the Sacred Heart of Milan - Department of Economics and Business Administration, Catholic University of the Sacred Heart of Milan - Department of Economics and Business Administration and University of Parma - Dipartimento di Scienze Economiche e Aziendali

detail.title: How Do Sustainable Literacies Shape Individual Sustainable Behaviors? A European Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper examines the determinants of retail investors' sustainable literacy (SL) and sustainable financial literacy (SFL) and tests how these literacies influence sustainable behaviors, specifically sustainable consumer behavior and sustainable financial behavior. Our unique database, constructed through a European survey conducted between the end of 2024 and the beginning of 2025, comprises a nationally representative sample of 4,296 individuals from Finland, Germany, Italy, and Spain. Some retail investors' personal traits-specifically, financial literacy and sustainable preferencesrather than the socio-demographic and socioeconomic ones, are shown to drive SL and SFL significantly. However, individuals with high levels of both literacies are not all the same but exhibit different ages, income, country of residence, and religiosity. We also demonstrate that SL is a significant driver of sustainable consumer behavior, which in turn moderates the relationship between SFL and sustainable financial behavior. When disentangling SFL into its conceptual and procedural dimensions, they are both positively related to sustainable consumer behavior, but they differ in their interaction with sustainable consumer behavior.

title: Urban Building Energy Modelling of the Residential Stock in Statistical Area 7
affiliations: Politecnico di Torino, Politecnico di Torino, Politecnico di Torino and Politecnico di Torino

detail.title: Urban Building Energy Modelling of the Residential Stock in Statistical Area 7
detail.abstract:
This study applies a GIS-based Urban Building Energy Modelling (UBEM) workflow to analyze the energy performance of the residential building stock in Statistical Area 7 (Borgo Nuovo), Turin. Characterized by a dense historic fabric and pre-1970 construction, the district exhibits high baseline energy consumption for space heating. The research evaluates the technical and economic impact of five retrofit scenarios: window replacement, roof insulation, floor insulation, external wall insulation, and a deep renovation combining all measures.

The analysis utilizes the BDTRE database and ISTAT census data to estimate heat losses based on building geometry and construction periods. Results indicate that the baseline stock performs poorly, with most buildings falling into energy classes E, F, and G. While deep renovation offers the highest energy and emission reductions—shifting most buildings to energy classes A and B—it presents prohibitive payback times without fiscal support. Among single-measure interventions, roof and wall insulation provide the most favorable cost-benefit ratios. The study highlights the critical role of fiscal incentives (such as the 50% and 36% tax bonuses) in making deep decarbonization strategies economically viable in historic urban contexts.

title: Supporting Young Homebuyers
affiliations: ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research and Maastricht University

detail.title: Supporting Young Homebuyers
detail.abstract: Many countries support young homebuyers financially, but the effects of such targeted policies on homeownership, efficiency, and welfare are not well understood. We study a high-profile transfer tax exemption for young homebuyers introduced in the Netherlands in 2021. The reform offers quasi-experimental variation across time, buyers, and housing units, which we exploit using multiple identification strategies and high-quality administrative data. The policy substantially increased housing transactions, but we can exclude even modest effects on overall homeownership. Instead, we document large timing responses, with bunching around key policy dates and the age threshold. We also show that more than half of the exemption was capitalized into house prices, benefitting sellers rather than buyers. To assess the policy's welfare implications, we use our reduced-form estimates in a simple assignment model with indivisible housing. While the exemption increased economic surplus, the gains accrued primarily to upper-middle-class households, raising doubts about the policy's effectiveness as a tool for improving social welfare.

title: On the Anatomy of Trend
affiliations: ATP

detail.title: On the Anatomy of Trend
detail.abstract: We present a theoretical framework for analyzing the performance of time-series momentum (trend-following) strategies when the underlying asset follows a general stationary Gaussian process. We derive closed-form expressions for the unconditional expected log payoff, decomposing the performance into a drift component related to the expected position and a timing component related to the alignment of the trend signal and the subsequent return of the underlying. Extending the analysis to conditional performance, we show that the conditional expected payoff preserves the characteristics from the unconditional: a conditional expected position component and a conditional timing component. We derive exact asymptotic limits for the conditional payoff in "deep crash" scenarios over a fixed horizon and show that even with i.i.d. returns, the conditional expected return is positive if the drawdown period is larger than one day. Finally, we show that a sufficiently long and severe drawdown always yields positive trend performance-irrespective of the underlying autocorrelation structure. We also characterize the role of the lookback parameter, revealing a trade-off between expected returns and hedge effectiveness. Empirical analysis of 103 assets over 25 years confirms the key theoretical predictions with rigorous statistical significance. We document a strongly convex conditional payoff profile ("smile"), quantify the "cost of convexity".

title: Generative Machine Learning in Professional Work and Professional Service Firms: A Research Agenda
affiliations: Lancaster University, Aalborg University, Stockholm School of Economics, University of Groningen, OsloMet - Oslo Metropolitan University and Lancaster University, Lancaster University

detail.title: Generative Machine Learning in Professional Work and Professional Service Firms: A Research Agenda
detail.abstract: This paper addresses the need for an approach to theorizing professional work and professional service firms in the generative machine learning age. We develop an approach using insights from existing literature on digital, algorithmic and artificial intelligence technologies. We seek to extend existing theories whilst also responding to the distinctive characteristics of generative machine learning and the implications for how we theorize change. We argue that an approach is needed focused on emerging and future interdependencies between professionals and generative machine learning, something that implies extending but also reimagining theoretical perspectives on expertise, work and organizations.

title: Green Money Talks: Responsible Ownership and Disclosure of Material Climate Commitments
affiliations: ICMA Centre, Henley Business School, University of Reading, ICMA Centre - Henley Business School, University of Reading and ICMA Centre, Henley Business School, University of Reading

detail.title: Green Money Talks: Responsible Ownership and Disclosure of Material Climate Commitments
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of institutional investors committed to the United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UN PRI) on the decision of UK rms to voluntarily disclose material climate commitments. Using ClimateBERT-based classications, we nd that UN PRI investors elicit investee rms to disclose material climate commitments, particularly those addressing transition risks rather than physical climate risks. Further tests based on exogenous FTSE 350 index inclusions and a dierence-in-dierences design exploiting the 20132014 UK duciary duty reform conrm these results, suggesting the relationship is likely causal. Moreover, we show that these UN PRI investor-induced disclosures have information content, as they are associated with positive absolute abnormal returns around report lings and improved analyst forecast accuracy. Overall, our results suggest that UN PRI investors not only function as active stewards driving rms to voluntarily disclose material climate commitments, but also that these disclosures improve price discovery and informational eciency in capital markets.

title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Competition Policy Standards
affiliations: University College London - Faculty of Laws and Athens University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Competition Policy Standards

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial conflict of interest. Ioannis Lianos was the President of the Hellenic Competition Commission and member of the OECD Competition Committee Bureau when the paper was drafted. Chrysovalantou Milliou is a member of the Hellenic Competition Commission.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding received for this paper.

detail.abstract: The contribution (to an OECD discussion) on competition policy standards aims to explore the various ‘competition policy standards’ put forward by the literature, by examining their respective advantages and disadvantages. It is important to acknowledge that the debate over ‘standards’ should not be dissociated from the broader. question of the goal(s) of the specific competition law and will inevitably have to tackle the institutional characteristics and capabilities of the specific enforcement system. Indeed, one may adopt a different approach concerning ‘competition policy standards’ in a competition law system that relies on enforcement by an integrated competition and market agency (i.e. combining roles of competition authority, sector-specific regulator and consumer protection), or on an integrated competition authority (only focusing on competition law enforcement) or on enforcement mainly by generalist or specialized courts (quasi- prosecutorial or prosecutorial systems of enforcement). Similarly, one may implement a different ‘competition policy standard’ for some markets with a strong polycentric dimension, to the extent that they may be considered as involving basic or sensitive for human well-being (or other public interest reasons) products, which reflect the societal choices of the specific polity. Competition authorities most often will use a toolkit approach that would take into account the overall legal framework and the characteristics of the specific market(s) before selecting the ‘policy standard’ that ‘fits’ the occasion. Guaranteeing consistency and transparency in the implementation of these standards, as well as following the broader directions provided by the legislator or the constitution, and drawing on a social contract approach, seems to us the most defensible position, from the perspective both of democratic governance and efficiency.

title: Optimal Transparency With (Out) Central Bank Intervention Under Fragmented Information: A Note
affiliations: University of Sousse, Faculty of Economic and Management Sciences of Sousse

detail.title: Optimal Transparency With (Out) Central Bank Intervention Under Fragmented Information: A Note
detail.abstract: We analyze the welfare consequences of a partial transparency strategy through the disclosure of fragmented public information in a beauty contest setting. The framework allows for possible policymaker intervention. In the absence of policy intervention, fragmented information is always welfare-deteriorating. In the presence of a stabilization policy, and depending on the coordination motive and the precision of the signals' range, less precise fragmented information might be the optimal strategy. In all cases, the expected loss values of the private sector converge for 𝑛 ≥ 4. Regardless of whether policy intervention exists or is absent, there is always a trade-off between less precise full public information and more accurate fragmented information if the central bank opts for partial transparency.

title: Exchange Rate shocks and Agri-trade Competitiveness under a Climate Change World: New Measure and Empirical Evidence
affiliations: University of Sousse, Faculty of Economic and Management Sciences of Sousse

detail.title: Exchange Rate shocks and Agri-trade Competitiveness under a Climate Change World: New Measure and Empirical Evidence
detail.abstract: This study explores the asymmetric effects of exchange rates and per capita CO2 emissions on Tunisia's agricultural competitiveness using unit root tests, cointegration analysis, the Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag model, and Toda-Yamamoto Granger causality. By constructing new competitiveness metrics, the study finds that positive exchange rate shifts boost competitiveness by lowering export costs, while negative shifts have mixed effects. Rising CO2 emissions, often linked to industrial growth, can enhance productivity, though the Composite Revealed Comparative Advantage (CRCA) shows decreased competitiveness with higher emissions, highlighting disparities in measurement's properties. These findings highlight the economic-environmental tradeoffs in Tunisia's agriculture, offering insights for policymakers aiming to improve sector performance while addressing environmental concerns and exchange rate volatility. This paper is a pioneering effort in establishing and comparing competitiveness measures in the agricultural sector in the Tunisian context and in analyzing the dual (asymmetric) impacts of exchange rates and climate change on agricultural competitiveness.

title: Macroeconomic Effects of Scheduled and Unscheduled Monetary Policy Surprises

detail.title: Macroeconomic Effects of Scheduled and Unscheduled Monetary Policy Surprises
detail.abstract: Using measures of monetary policy surprises from the Overnight Indexed Swap market in India, this paper documents heterogeneity in the effects of monetary policy surprises on scheduled and unscheduled announcement dates. Higher interest rates on scheduled announcement dates lower stock prices, reduce forecasted and actual output as well as inflation. In contrast, monetary policy surprises on unscheduled announcement dates are predictable by past macroeconomic conditions, and higher interest rates on these dates are found to raise stock prices, output and inflation on impact. Moreover, unscheduled announcements are found to frequently coincide with important macroeconomic data releases. These results are consistent with less precise identification of exogenous changes in monetary policy on unscheduled announcement dates compared to scheduled announcement dates. Monetary policy transmission to aggregate demand conditions in India, identified using monetary policy surprises on scheduled announcement dates, is found to be more theoretically consistent and significantly stronger than previously documented in the literature.

title: Estimation of Economy-Wide Rebound Effect: To What Extent Does the Aggregation of Regions and Sectors Matter?
affiliations: Center for International Climate and Environmental Research (CICERO)

detail.title: Estimation of Economy-Wide Rebound Effect: To What Extent Does the Aggregation of Regions and Sectors Matter?
detail.abstract: The rebound effect studies show considerable economy-wide rebound effects of energy efficiency gains on energy use. However, regions and production sectors in these studies are typically aggregated across the entire economy due to e.g., calculation capacity, time costs and data availability. This article explores to what extent the aggregation of regions and sectors may affect the estimated economy-wide rebound effect by using a global computable general equilibrium model. Results show that the aggregation of regions and sectors can only modestly bias the estimated global rebound effect, by less than 2.5% in the cases of this study. the aggregation of sectors tend to overestimate the rebound effects while it is unclear for the aggregation of regions. In the cases of the most disaggregated sectors, the bias due to the aggregation of regions tends to be considerably narrowed.

title: One Piece: Political Relations and Capital Flows Across the Taiwan Strait
affiliations: Xiamen University - Institute for Financial and Accounting Studies, Xiamen University and Xiamen University - Institute for Financial and Accounting Studies

detail.title: One Piece: Political Relations and Capital Flows Across the Taiwan Strait
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether the political relationship between mainland China and Taiwan influences firm-level investment behavior across the Strait. To capture this relationship, we construct a novel text-based political index using transcripts from the Taiwan Affairs Office. Our findings indicate a positive association between Cross-Strait political relations and capital inflows from Taiwan. To strengthen causal inference, we develop a novel instrumental variable based on third-party diplomatic relationships. Furthermore, we show that public self-identification and economic development are key drivers of this phenomenon, whereas government policies on both sides play a limited role. We also find that regions with strong economic ties to mainland China serve as major destinations for global capital flows when political index is high. Overall, our study provides important insights for policymakers and business leaders seeking to manage the Taiwan question and promote a stable and peaceful regional environment.

title: Private Innovation and Wealth Inequality
affiliations: and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), Swedish House of Finance

detail.title: Private Innovation and Wealth Inequality

declarations.funderStatement: Funded by the European Union. Views and opinions expressed are, however, those of the author(s) only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or the European Research Council Executive Agency. Neither the European Union nor the granting authority can be held responsible for them.

detail.abstract: Wealth inequality has risen sharply in recent decades. We study how restricted access to private firm innovation contributes to this rise using a structural model of wealth accumulation with scale dependence. We construct a new long-run measure of innovation value that includes both public and private firms and document a pronounced shift of value creation toward private firms, whose equity is concentrated among high-wealth individuals. Calibrated to the 1979 wealth distribution, the model shows that exclusive access to private-firm innovation accounts for between half and two-thirds of the subsequent increase in the top 1% wealth share.

title: Do Firms Manipulate their Carbon Emissions Reporting?
affiliations: , University of Washington and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Do Firms Manipulate their Carbon Emissions Reporting?
detail.abstract: We document that firms underreport carbon emissions in the aftermath of firm-specific, high-profile climate controversies. To tie underreporting to manipulation, we show that firms underreport more when they avoid costly decarbonization, enjoy greater reporting discretion, and experience greater stakeholder backlash. Additional analysis suggests that firms manipulate primarily to avoid reputational damage. Following controversies, firms increase their use of third-party assurance, consistent with attempts to bolster the credibility of reported emissions. Yet such assurance does not reduce subsequent underreporting unless board oversight exists. In another setting, we additionally find evidence that firms selectively apply carbon accounting rules to restate historical emissions in ways that create favorable trends. Together, we provide large sample evidence consistent with firms intentionally misreporting their carbon emissions.

title: Hiring External or Internal Talent? Business Education Leadership in Higher Education
affiliations: Illinois Wesleyan University

detail.title: Hiring External or Internal Talent? Business Education Leadership in Higher Education

declarations.ethicsApproval: The work does not involve human subject research.

detail.abstract: I examine whether the appointment of internal versus external deans affects enrollment in business schools at large public universities in the United States. Using leadership transitions at 73 business schools from 2008-09 through 2022-23 and enrollment data, I employ a stacked difference-in-differences identification strategy. The appointment of a new dean has a small and statistically insignificant effect on business school enrollment. However, estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity by hire type: internal appointments are associated with enrollment growth of approximately 5-6 percent per year, whereas external appointments are associated with no meaningful change. These effects are present in both undergraduate and graduate programs and lead to increases in business schools’ share of total university enrollment. The findings indicate that, on the key performance indicator of enrollment, internal hires outperform external ones in this context.

title: Multi-Task Gaussian Processes for Tactical Execution Under Regime Shifts
affiliations: University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance, University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance and Scuola Normale Superiore

detail.title: Multi-Task Gaussian Processes for Tactical Execution Under Regime Shifts
detail.abstract: In electronic markets, broker execution algorithms comprise a strategic layer that sets a trading schedule and a tactical layer that optimise child-order execution. This paper introduces the Multi-Task Gaussian Process bandit with Likelihood Ratio test (MTGP-LR) for the tactical layer. MTGP-LR maps market features to trading actions, adapts to regime shifts through change point detection, and employs a kernel that transfers learning across related actions. In stationary markets, MTGP-LR achieves sublinear regret. In nonstationary markets, we show how to control inference error and provide guarantees for detection delay. Our main result derives high-probability regret bounds in regime-switching markets. We illustrate the framework in two applications: child market orders timing and child limit order placement. Without assumptions on dynamics or regime transitions, MTGP-LR is accurate, computationally efficient, and outperforms control-based models when brokers misspecify model parameters.

title: Regional Inequality Analysis: A Case of Scotland’s MUP Resulting from Continuous Did and Did Evaluation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Regional Inequality Analysis: A Case of Scotland’s MUP Resulting from Continuous Did and Did Evaluation
detail.abstract: Scotland’s MUP witnessing huge impediments along the way, with its’ introduction in 2018, has seen a reduction in alcohol-related hospital admissions. The policy was intended to curb down the alcoholic consumption among harmful drinkers. However, while the policy is set to address the consumption levels, the deprivation regions in Scotland widen the scope of the policy being effective among highly deprived regions. This paper examines the MUP’s effectiveness by considering the alcohol- related hospital admissions among the deprived regions in Scotland, with a strong hypothesis that less deprived regions are less affected by the policy implementation. The use of continuous DiD with Scotland’s Council data has been employed with additional data from England’s Unitary Authorities on the alcohol-related hospital admissions, comparing that of Scotland’s admissions, resulting in a triple DiD analysis, performed to capture the causal inference of the policy. Moreover, the least deprived, the medium deprived, and the most deprived councils in Scotland were compared with those of England’s UAs, widening our understanding of the policy effects on these specific deprived regions. On the whole, a 16% drop in the alcohol- related hospital admissions was noticed in Scotland and a 7% drop in the admissions compared with England during the same period. That said, the Did terms, supposed to capture the policy effects, turned out to be insignificant, pointing out the fact that the aggregate council-level data failed to explain the regional variation among the councils in Scotland.

title: Who is an Employee? The Unfortunate Tax and Superannuation Legacy of a Transplanted Category
affiliations: Curtin University - Curtin Law School and University of Western Australia Law School

detail.title: Who is an Employee? The Unfortunate Tax and Superannuation Legacy of a Transplanted Category
detail.abstract: In the absence of statutory definitions of terms used in modern statutes, common law judges will rely on longstanding meanings imported from long-established areas of common law, a phenomenon known as transplanted categories. A notable example in Commonwealth income tax and superannuation legislation is the transplantation of the common law definition of an employee from vicarious liability tort law into four areas of modern tax and superannuation law. The tests developed by the courts to distinguish employees from independent contractors in tort law, including control over the work process and a distinction between remuneration based on results or hours worked, have no correspondence with rationale for distinguishing employees from contractors in income tax or superannuation law. A review of the history of the incorporation of a tort law definition into income tax and superannuation law shows courts shied away from purposive interpretations that might have achieved the policy objectives of the distinction. The optimal reform path may be to abandon entirely a distinction based on the characterisation of a person providing personal labour services and instead legislate a simple formula that achieves directly the policy objective in the classification of individual service providers.

title: Envisioning Africa's Future: A Pathway to Sustainable Development and Unity
affiliations: Durban University of Technology and Durban University of Technology (DUT)

detail.title: Envisioning Africa's Future: A Pathway to Sustainable Development and Unity
detail.abstract: "Envisioning Africa's Future: A Pathway to Sustainable Development and Unity" explores the transformative visions and strategic frameworks necessary for achieving sustainable development across the African continent. As Africa grapples with multifaceted challenges ranging from socioeconomic disparities and climate change to political instability and health crises, the need for a cohesive strategy that prioritizes unity and collaboration among nations is more pressing than ever. This paper argues that sustainable development in Africa requires not only innovative policies and practices but also the empowerment of local communities and stakeholders. This systematic qualitative method aimed to explore the Envisioning Africa's Future: A Pathway to Sustainable Development and Unity. The methodology involved a structured approach gathering and analysing qualitative data from relevant online literature sources, and expert opinions. Selection of articles focused on peer-reviewed 28 articles from 1962 to 2023 that discussed the Envisioning Africa's Future: A Pathway to Sustainable Development and Unity. Data was categorised as the Migration patterns, their Impact on Southern African communities. This systematic approach aimed to provide insights into the Envisioning Africa's Future: A Pathway to Sustainable Development and Unity. The role of youth, women, and marginalized communities in driving sustainable change is also highlighted, advocating for grassroots involvement in decision-making processes. The findings suggest that a shared vision for Africa's future, grounded in the principles of sustainability, equity, and unity, can mobilize collective action and foster resilience against contemporary challenges. Ultimately, this paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discourse on Africa's development trajectory, presenting actionable insights for policymakers, scholars, and civil society aimed at realizing a prosperous and united Africa. Through collaborative efforts and visionary leadership, the continent can harness its rich resources and human capital to create a sustainable and inclusive future for all its citizens.
